title: China’s auto industry and global overcapacity
text:
Car industry is fascinating and difficult to understand the winners and losers!

The simple version: China built far more car factories than its own people will buy cars, so it’s dumping the extra cars on the rest of the world very cheaply.

The core economics

China has capacity to make about 63 million vehicles a year, but Chinese buyers will purchase only around 18.5 million this year. That’s a huge oversupply. Normally, a market this overbuilt would see weak companies go bankrupt and factories close. That isn’t happening because local governments own stakes, subsidize factories, and don’t want the job losses. So, companies keep producing, prices fall, and the surplus gets exported (about 12 million vehicles this year, up from roughly 1 million at the start of the decade).

China

Losers: Most Chinese carmakers. Profit margins are down to 3.6%, prices are down almost 20% since 2023, and “zombie” brands like Skyworth sell almost nothing. Local governments that poured in money also lose, as do the workers whose jobs depend on factories that shouldn’t exist. NIO has lost over $1 billion a year, for example.

Winners: The strongest firms (BYD, CATL, Geely) are forcing innovation, like batteries that charge in under 10 minutes. Chinese consumers also win from cheaper, better cars. And as a country, China gains export power and technological leadership in EVs.

The big picture is a mixed one: China wins as an industrial power, but its car industry is losing money at home.

Europe

Losers: European automakers. Volkswagen is cutting up to 50,000 jobs, BMW about 8,000, and Stellantis is losing money in Europe. They’re hit twice: they’re losing sales inside China, and they face Chinese competitors at home. VW’s CEO said Chinese price points can’t be matched with European cost structures. Autoworkers and the communities around these plants are the most exposed.

Winners: European car buyers. A BYD Seal in the UK costs roughly $10,000 less than a comparable VW Passat. Chinese brands already hold 11.7% of the European market.

United States

Winners: US automakers like GM and Ford, because tariffs and tech restrictions have basically locked Chinese cars out, protecting their profits. They also still have a China presence (GM just extended its joint venture there for 20 years).

Loser (indirectly): American car buyers, who don’t get access to cheap Chinese cars. The article doesn’t dwell on this, but it’s the flip side of protection: higher prices and less competitive pressure.

One-line summary

The article’s central point is that the “shakeout” China needs hasn’t started. Until weak companies fail or capacity gets cut, China will keep pushing cheap cars abroad, which means the pressure on Europe is likely to grow, not fade. The US is shielded for now by policy, not by being more competitive.

title: Reflections on the Elizabeth Holmes movie
text:
We just saw The Elizabeth Holmes Movie — You Can See Everything (2026) in the theater (more people actively participating in a movie theater I have ever seen)!

My take:  I couldn't quite figure out "who is zooming whom", who is lying or being duped, or who the joke is on. The parties are Liz Holmes, her partner Evans (who "manages" her and started another company), the film makers (Nathan and Lance), or the watching audience (the general public). All of these are blended, without any objective truth, and a general discordance between what you see and what you get.  Holmes comes across as completely sweet with a placid-affect on intimate close-ups (with brief tears) despite awaiting an 11-year prison sentence while breast-feeding her infant. She has no harshness or evidence of evil wrongdoing, or any self-awareness. Evans comes across as the manipulator and self-aggrandizing. 

The current major film about Elizabeth Holmes is the 2026 A24 documentary You Can See Everything, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, which follows her 34 days before prison and blends intimate access with surreal, metaâdocumentary elements. 

Overview

You Can See Everything premiered at the Telluride Film Festival in September 2026 and was released in U.S. theaters on October 16, 2026. It is a metaâdocumentary that documents Holmes and her partner Billy Evans at a rented beach house in Del Mar, California, in the weeks before Holmes began her 11âyear federal prison sentence for defrauding investors in her bloodâtesting company Theranos. 

Core premise: Fielder and Oppenheim move in with Holmes and Evans for 34 days, filming their daily life, public defenses, and private interactions 
Tone: The film mixes trueâcrime storytelling with Fielder’s signature cringeâcomedy and surreal framing, often breaking the fourth wall and using humor to highlight the tension between Holmes’s claims and the public’s skepticism 
Key moments: Holmes denies intentionally lying about Theranos’s device, while Evans manages her public image. Fielder confronts them about the device’s capabilities, and Holmes even has her body 3Dâscanned before prison 

Extended journey: Filming continues for two years after Holmes’s incarceration, following Evans’s new company Haemanthus 
Production and Reception
Directors: Nathan Fielder (feature debut) and Lance Oppenheim 
Production: A24, with a reported $7 million budget and over $45 million box office 

Critical response: Critics praise its originality, depth, and unsettling blend of intimacy and abstraction; some find it long or deliberately opaque 
Cultural impact: The film has reignited public debate over Holmes’s portrayal, with the whistleblower Tyler Shultz claiming Fielder omitted key facts for artistic effect.

title: AI, artificial intimacy, and human relationships
text:
AI, Artificial Intimacy, and the Future of Human Relationships

This is a summary of Ezra Klein’s conversation with MIT sociologist Sherry Turkle, author of Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines.

I found Turkle to be way too pessimistic!  I agree children are off limits, but adults will need to make their own decisions AND we will need long term data as to "outcomes."  Are we doing a social experiment and releasing this technology to the unwary public, surely. I am not aware of a model whereby we can do controlled trial evaluation (a la FDA) prior to deployment (can be argued).

Central argument

Artificial intelligence is transforming human relationships, not simply by providing information but by simulating emotional intimacy. Sherry Turkle argues that the greatest danger is not that AI will become humanlike, but that humans will increasingly prefer artificial relationships to the complexity, vulnerability, and unpredictability of real ones. Ezra Klein shares many of her concerns but challenges her pessimism, arguing that AI can provide genuine psychological and practical benefits even without possessing consciousness or human emotions.

The major arguments

1. AI exploits fundamental human vulnerabilities. Turkle traces the phenomenon to ELIZA, a primitive 1960s chatbot whose users developed emotional attachments despite knowing it understood nothing. Today's sophisticated systems amplify this ELIZA effect through personalized, responsive, seemingly empathetic conversation. Unlike earlier technologies that competed for attention, AI companions compete for emotional attachment. Turkle calls this a particularly troubling form of technological seduction.

2. AI may weaken our capacity for human relationships. Real relationships require disagreement, compromise, patience, and emotional discomfort. Chatbots, by contrast, are generally accommodating, available, and affirming. Turkle worries that repeated exposure to these frictionless interactions will diminish our tolerance for imperfect human relationships. Klein agrees that the disappearance of interpersonal friction could undermine not only personal development but also the ability to engage constructively with disagreement in a democracy.

3. The therapeutic potential creates a genuine dilemma. Klein makes the strongest counterargument: AI can offer affordable, immediate, nonjudgmental support to people who lack access to therapists, companionship, or meaningful conversation. If an AI intervention reduces loneliness, improves coping skills, or helps someone navigate relationships, shouldn't those outcomes matter more than whether the machine genuinely cares? Turkle responds that human therapy involves authentic concern, accountability, and mutual recognition—qualities AI cannot replicate. Both acknowledge that AI can be useful as a coach, intellectual partner, or educational resource.

4. Children represent the greatest concern. Turkle argues that children develop emotional maturity through relationships involving genuine reciprocity, frustration, and vulnerability. AI companions that simulate affection could interfere with this development. Klein agrees that deploying emotionally persuasive AI to children without adequate evidence of safety resembles society's earlier, poorly controlled experiment with social media. Both favor stronger protections, although they differ on whether AI might also improve children's social skills.

5. Commercial incentives could magnify the harm. The conversation identifies a structural problem: companies may ultimately profit from maximizing users' emotional engagement. Personalized AI companions could become instruments of behavioral manipulation, commercial persuasion, and dependency. Turkle connects this to a broader deterioration of community institutions and face-to-face relationships. Her proposed response is not abandoning AI, but rebuilding human connections while resisting the commercialization of artificial intimacy.

Critical assessment

Turkle's argument is strongest in identifying the psychological mechanisms of attachment and the potential conflict between commercial incentives and human well-being. Her distinction between AI as a tool and AI as a substitute for human relationships is particularly valuable. The concerns about children, emotional dependency, and manipulative design deserve serious attention.

However, her conclusions sometimes exceed the evidence presented. Much of her argument rests on qualitative interviews, psychological theory, and extrapolation from social media rather than longitudinal studies demonstrating that AI companionship causes social deterioration. She also risks creating a false dichotomy between authentic human relationships and artificial ones. A person can recognize that AI lacks subjective experience while still deriving substantial intellectual, emotional, or therapeutic benefit from interacting with it.

Klein's most compelling challenge is that the value of an interaction should be judged partly by its outcomes, not solely by the nature of the entity providing it. AI could supplement rather than displace relationships, especially for isolated older adults, socially anxious individuals, and people with limited access to professional services. Turkle does not fully resolve this objection.

A further weakness is the tendency to treat AI systems as uniformly sycophantic and commercially driven. Their behavior depends on design, training, safeguards, and user preferences. The discussion would benefit from clearer distinctions among AI companions, therapeutic tools, educational assistants, and general-purpose systems.

Conclusion

The interview raises a profound question: Will AI expand our capacity to participate in human life, or provide an increasingly attractive escape from it?
The most defensible position lies between Turkle's alarm and technological optimism. AI should be evaluated by measurable outcomes: psychological well-being, social connectedness, independence, and interpersonal competence. Particular caution is justified for children and emotionally vulnerable users.

The goal should not be to prohibit artificial companionship categorically, but to develop AI that strengthens human agency and real-world relationships rather than encouraging dependency.

Bottom line: AI's greatest social risk may not be that machines become too human, but that people gradually lose the motivation and skills to engage with one another. That is a serious hypothesis—one deserving rigorous research, thoughtful regulation, and careful technological design, rather than either unquestioning acceptance or categorical rejection.

title: Business schools, leadership, and the public good
text:
Highly interesting editorial in the NYT, about business schools and MBAs, that is unflattering and has implications for our politics, our economy, and balance between labor and capital (public good vs. private good).

Central thesis: Business schools have become highly effective at producing financially successful managers but insufficiently concerned with producing socially responsible leaders. Marquis believes that changing this requires redesigning the institution itself, not merely adding ethics to the curriculum.

Business schools have become institutions that prioritize profit maximization over broader societal interests, argues Chris Marquis, a Cambridge business professor with more than 20 years of experience at Harvard, Cornell and Cambridge. Although many students enter with aspirations to improve society, business education frequently redirects their ambitions toward lucrative careers in finance and consulting. Marquis cites research showing that companies led by business-educated managers tend to reduce wages and labor’s share of income without corresponding improvements in productivity, investment or growth. He argues that business schools do more than reflect corporate capitalism: They actively perpetuate a worldview that elevates shareholder returns, executive power and private gain over workers, communities and the environment.

The teaching methods themselves reinforce these priorities. Marquis criticizes the celebrated Harvard case-study approach for presenting simplified, often company-approved narratives that glorify executives while neglecting systemic problems, competing perspectives and corporate failures. He argues that popular concepts such as stakeholder capitalism and corporate social responsibility frequently serve as public-relations exercises rather than meaningful reforms. Beyond business schools, this market-driven mentality has increasingly permeated universities, where rankings, fundraising, career earnings and institutional profitability displace the traditional missions of critical inquiry, intellectual independence and liberal education.

Marquis concludes that business schools need fundamental replacement, not incremental reform. Ethics electives and sustainability programs cannot overcome institutions structurally designed to advance private economic interests. Instead, he advocates interdisciplinary schools focused on how organizations serve society, incorporating economics, sociology, history, public policy and environmental sustainability. Such institutions would examine corporations alongside cooperatives, unions and nonprofit organizations, emphasizing how economic systems distribute power, risks and rewards. His central argument is not that business education should disappear, but that it should be rebuilt around the public good rather than shareholder wealth.

title: Lifelong learning through OLLI
text:
I am aware of the Osher Lifelong Learning Program (OLLI). It appears to be an outstanding program for those interested in ongoing education in a broad array of subjects, especially for those on the verge of retirement! OLLI is linked to various local universities around the country; programs are hybrid being both in-person at local venues as well as online. One aspect of becoming a member is the opportunity to be a speaker, sharing your expertise in your discipline.

In this context, I highly suggest this lecture by my cousin, Dr. Krishna Kavi a retired Emeritus Professor and Chairman of Computer Science at University of North Texas in Dallas. This is an hour-long dissection of all things AI, including how it developed, how it works, and of course all of the current concerns about safety. The speaker is engaging, current, and uses humor.

title: Autonomous AI and the future of healthcare
text:
Trump administration Integrating AI into healthcare: what can go wrong? 

My thinking involves comparing autonomous vehicles (Waymo, Zoox, Tesla Robotaxi) with "autonomous AI doctors".  There will be risks and mishaps during the deployment phase, but eventually, the benefits will far outweigh those risks. Many thoughtful people with subject matter expertise, as well as policymakers, will need to be involved. This will not happen overnight, there are serious financial incentives, turf battles, and industry winners and losers, but the general public needs to have overall better outcomes. With autonomous cars, the metric is fewer deaths; in healthcare, there are other metrics.

Medicine currently asks:   "When is AI good enough that we can safely remove the physician?"

Khosla / Zeke Emanuel's logic (addressed in a recent JAMA article referenced) ultimately invites a different question:   "Once AI becomes sufficiently capable, what evidence demonstrates that adding the physician makes care better?"

Those sound similar, but philosophically they are very different. 

The second treats the physician as another component of the health-care system whose incremental benefit must be demonstrated, rather than assuming human supervision is inherently beneficial. That is how I would design a clinical trial.

My personal bias is to stratify relative risks in medicine. Lack of access (insurance, out-of-pocket costs, provider shortages) is a major problem that leads to bad outcomes. Also, many provider visits are for "trivial" complaints or conditions in primary care, in fact there has been an explosion in non-physician nurse or PA providers. What "evidence" supported the safety of allowing non-physicians to provide care?  Those on the inside (without conflicts) routinely accept them as adequate providers. So, in primary care, many of the routine diagnoses can readily be automated by agentic AI. 

The barriers will be patient acceptance and trust, and pushback from professional organizations to protect their turf! And of course, there is the money issue.  Common diagnoses such as hypertension, lipid disorders, diabetes, depression, low back pain, cough, and allergies/sinus troubles are examples where a clear algorithm or decision tree (with specific call outs for escalation) works well. Based on pricing / convenience, people will gradually flock to them (imho). As an example, our Amazon Prime account now offers One Medical, which we signed up for.  People are routinely using driverless cars where available, human-less financial transactions, etc.

Over time, I fully support this direction. Of course, it needs oversight, outcome data capture, and some regulations. And gradual deployment over a decade or more.

This was wholly written by me and not by an AI agent.

title: Public health and political leadership
text:
I found El-Sayed to be an extraordinarily thoughtful public health physician and a deft politician and an American to the core, despite attempts by his opponents to "otherize" him! Born in MI, captain of several high school sports teams, commencement speaker at Univ of MI (lauded by Bill Clinton at the time), a physician and a Rhodes Scholar. Now running for the US Senate at age 41.

The health-care section is the intellectual center of the interview with Ezra Klein. What makes it interesting is that Abdul El-Sayed is not simply arguing that “health care should be free,” and Ezra Klein does not really defend the existing system. They largely agree on the diagnosis—American health care is extraordinarily expensive, administratively cumbersome, and often hostile to patients. Their disagreement is over how much of the system Medicare for All can realistically replace, what cost controls it would require, and whether Americans would accept the transition. The transcript explicitly frames the choice as rebuilding Obamacare versus moving toward “Medicare for all or Medicare for more.”

The strongest El-Sayed argument is not that government inherently runs health care better than markets. It is that the United States has constructed a health-care market in which normal competitive mechanisms don't work particularly well. Patients cannot shop effectively when sick; prices are opaque; insurers and hospital systems consolidate; employer-based coverage limits consumer mobility; and providers spend enormous resources negotiating and administering multiple payment systems.

Klein's strongest response is that single payer doesn't magically solve the resource constraint. Once everyone has comprehensive insurance with minimal cost sharing, demand rises. Savings then require either lower provider/drug prices, reduced utilization, administrative savings—or some combination. Push prices too low and you risk shortages, hospital stress and slower innovation. Keep reimbursement high and the promised savings shrink.

That leaves what I think is the most important implication of their discussion for the United States:

The real emerging policy question may no longer be “Medicare for All: yes or no?” It may be how far the United States should move the financing of health care away from fragmented employer/private insurance toward universal public coverage—and how quickly.

In that sense, the interview suggests that “Medicare for More” may be the bridge between the ACA system and single payer: strengthen traditional Medicare, expand its benefits, gradually lower the eligibility age, possibly cover children, allow supplemental private coverage, and observe what happens to cost, access, provider participation and public acceptance before moving farther.

That is much more incremental than the 2020 version of Medicare for All, while retaining El-Sayed's fundamental objective: make public insurance the floor beneath the entire American health-care system rather than a safety net available mainly at particular ages or income levels.

I personally think that an incremental message will garner more public support and is winnable at the ballot box!

title: Medical aid in dying and patient autonomy
text:
This topic of Medical Aid in Dying (MAID) is not a fun topic, we have been talking about it for decades, but this is gradually playing out across the US at the state level, in a predictable red vs. blue map (similar to abortion and other divisive topics). Notice the difference between NY/NJ vs. PA next door.  

The recent *Freakonomics Radio* episode, "Who Gets to Choose a âGood Death’?”", uses New York’s new Medical Aid in Dying law to explore an issue that is simultaneously medical, legal, ethical, religious, and intensely personal. Stephen Dubner speaks with Governor Kathy Hochul, economist Al Roth, death doula Suzanne O’Brien, and physician-ethicist Daniel Sulmasy. Their disagreement illustrates why this issue does not divide neatly into compassionate versus uncompassionate camps. Both sides invoke compassion, dignity, and protection of patients; they disagree about what those principles require.

What New York has done

Governor Hochul signed New York’s Medical Aid in Dying Act in February 2026, and it took effect August 5. It permits an adult New York resident with an incurable and irreversible terminal illness expected to cause death within six months to request medication to end his or her life.

Importantly, this is **not euthanasia**: the physician does not administer the medication. The patient must have decision-making capacity and must self-administer it.

New York built in substantial safeguards. Two physicians must confirm the terminal diagnosis and capacity; a psychiatrist or psychologist evaluates capacity; the patient makes oral and written requests; witnesses are required; hospice, palliative care and other alternatives must be discussed; and participation by physicians is voluntary.

So this is not about unrestricted suicide or doctors deciding whose lives are worth living. The question is narrower: **Should a competent adult already dying from a terminal disease be permitted to determine when and how that final dying process ends?**

The American legal framework

There is no federal constitutional right to medical aid in dying, but neither does the Constitution prohibit states from allowing it.

The Supreme Court established this framework in two unanimous 1997 decisions. In *Washington v. Glucksberg*, it held that physician-assisted suicide is not a fundamental liberty protected by the Fourteenth Amendment, so states may prohibit it. In *Vacco v. Quill*, the Court upheld New York’s prohibition and recognized a legal distinction between refusing life-sustaining treatment and providing medication intended to cause death.

The practical result is federalism: states largely decide. Ironically, nearly 30 years after the Supreme Court upheld New York’s authority to prohibit assisted dying, New York’s elected government has chosen to permit it under tightly controlled circumstances. The Constitution accommodates either decision.

Federal law also restricts the use of federal funds for services intended to cause or assist death. Meanwhile, MAID has gradually expanded through state legislation, ballot initiatives and court decisions.

The Hippocratic dilemma

For physicians, there is another tension. The original Hippocratic Oath was remarkably explicit: a physician pledged not to provide a deadly drug when asked or suggest such a course. This is historically more precise than the familiar phrase “First, do no harm,” which does not literally appear in the Oath.

The traditional principle is powerful: **the physician is a healer, not an agent of death.** Patients should trust that physicians will relieve suffering, stop futile treatment and accompany them through dying—but never intentionally help cause their death.

The AMA still formally opposes physician-assisted suicide, describing it as incompatible with the physician’s role as healer and warning of societal risks. Yet it also recognizes a genuine moral conflict and that conscientious physicians can reach different conclusions.

Modern medicine has further complicated the distinction. A competent patient can refuse a ventilator, dialysis, chemotherapy, artificial nutrition or resuscitation even when death predictably follows. Physicians may withdraw life-sustaining treatment and, for otherwise uncontrollable suffering, use palliative sedation.

So where exactly is the ethical boundary?

The argument for medical aid in dying

The strongest argument combines autonomy with relief of suffering. If a competent adult may refuse treatment and thereby allow death, why should that same patient—already dying of metastatic cancer, ALS or another irreversible disease—not have some control over the timing and circumstances of an inevitable death?

There is also an important distinction between **prolonging life and prolonging dying**. Modern medicine has become extraordinarily successful at extending biological life, sometimes beyond the point at which patients believe that extension serves their interests.

Merely possessing the medication may also provide reassurance. A patient can obtain it and never use it (61% who have the tools do not). What has been restored is some control at a time when disease has progressively removed control over almost everything else.

The argument against

The objections deserve equal seriousness. Autonomy does not occur in a vacuum. A frail patient may feel like a financial or emotional burden. Someone without good hospice, home care, disability services or family support may technically “choose” death under circumstances that substantially constrain the choice.

There is also the boundary problem. If six months is acceptable, why not twelve? Why terminal physical illness but not unbearable chronic illness? What about early dementia, severe psychiatric disease, or an advance directive written while competent? Other countries have drawn these boundaries differently. Critics worry that an exceptional remedy can gradually become normalized.

And there is a broader societal question: **What happens when death becomes one of the options medicine can provide?** Opponents particularly worry about the elderly, disabled, poor and socially isolated. Supporters counter that carefully designed safeguards can protect vulnerable patients without denying autonomy to everyone else.

The real question

The *Freakonomics* episode ultimately raises two separate questions:

**Does a competent, terminally ill person have a legitimate interest in controlling the manner and timing of an imminent death?**

And:

**Can society construct a medical and legal system that respects that autonomy without creating unacceptable risks for vulnerable people?**

One can answer those questions differently.

For physicians, the dilemma is even sharper. The Hippocratic tradition asks us to relieve suffering and not cause death. Modern medical ethics adds a powerful third obligation: respect patient autonomy. Medical aid in dying can put those principles into direct tension.

Perhaps that is why **“Who Gets to Choose a Good Death?”** is exactly the right title. Modern medicine has acquired extraordinary power to postpone death. The harder question is who should ultimately control that power—the physician, government, society, or the competent patient whose life is ending?

Some physicians may wish to be advocates to champion this issue, buy my position is that of caution, trepidation, but in overall sympathy to the patient.

title: Big Tech and the East India Company analogy
text:
William Dalrymple, in the NYT Op-Ed, argues that today’s Big Tech companies are beginning to resemble the British East India Company: corporations so large and strategically important that they acquire quasi-sovereign power. His parallels are corporate lobbying and political influence, control of critical infrastructure, growing integration with the military, and governments becoming dependent on firms that may become “too big to fail.” He uses SpaceX/Starlink, Palantir, Google, Amazon and other AI companies as examples and argues that democratic governments need to reassert control before corporate and state interests become inseparable.

Where the analogy works—and where it fails

The lobbying/political-capture analogy is the strongest part. The East India Company used wealth and political connections to shape Parliament; modern tech firms spend heavily on lobbying and campaign politics and have extraordinary access to government. Likewise, dependence on privately owned infrastructure such as Starlink raises a legitimate question about how much strategic authority governments should delegate to corporations.

But Dalrymple stretches the analogy much too far.

The East India Company was literally a sovereign power. It collected taxes, minted money, operated courts, negotiated treaties, governed territory and commanded an army of roughly 200,000 men. Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, Meta and SpaceX do none of these things in any remotely comparable sense.
Market capitalization â  national economic power. Comparing Nvidia’s $5 trillion market value with Germany’s GDP is rhetorically dramatic but economically apples-to-oranges: market cap is the present valuation of a stock of corporate equity; GDP is one year's flow of national production.
Government contracting is not sovereignty. Palantir supplying targeting software or SpaceX providing communications makes these firms powerful defense contractors. It does not make them analogous to a company that independently conquered Bengal and subsequently governed millions of people.
The direction of power is importantly different. The U.S. government can regulate, tax, prosecute, break up, exclude from contracts or potentially nationalize strategically essential corporate assets. Dalrymple himself supplies evidence for this when describing the federal government's ability to punish Anthropic for refusing Pentagon demands.
Competition matters. The East India Company possessed a government-granted monopoly and territorial authority. Today's tech giants are extraordinarily powerful but compete with one another—OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, xAI, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia and others—and remain embedded in markets ultimately governed by states.
Most importantly, the EIC's fundamental business model became territorial conquest and extraction. Big Tech's power comes principally from intellectual property, networks, computing infrastructure, data and consumer/business adoption. That is an enormous qualitative difference, not merely a difference of degree.

Bottom line: Dalrymple identifies a genuine modern problem—private concentration of economically and strategically indispensable infrastructure can translate into political power. But the East India Company comparison works better as a warning metaphor than as a historical equivalence. The EIC was effectively a privatized colonial state with an army. Big Tech consists of exceptionally influential corporations operating within states that still possess overwhelming legal, fiscal and military supremacy. Conflating those two makes the article vivid, but also considerably overstates its case.

The U.S. government can regulate, tax, prosecute, break up, exclude from contracts or potentially nationalize strategically essential corporate assets. Dalrymple himself supplies evidence for this when describing the federal government's ability to punish Anthropic for refusing Pentagon demands.
Competition matters. The East India Company possessed a government-granted monopoly and territorial authority. Today's tech giants are extraordinarily powerful but compete with one another—OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, xAI, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia and others—and remain embedded in markets ultimately governed by states.
Most importantly, the EIC's fundamental business model became territorial conquest and extraction. Big Tech's power comes principally from intellectual property, networks, computing infrastructure, data and consumer/business adoption. That is an enormous qualitative difference, not merely a difference of degree.

Bottom line: Dalrymple identifies a genuine modern problem—private concentration of economically and strategically indispensable infrastructure can translate into political power. But the East India Company comparison works better as a warning metaphor than as a historical equivalence. The EIC was effectively a privatized colonial state with an army. Big Tech consists of exceptionally influential corporations operating within states that still possess overwhelming legal, fiscal and military supremacy. Conflating those two makes the article vivid, but also considerably overstates its case.

title: The evolving US–China economic competition
text:
This is an informative discussion about the US - China competition and how it has evolved over the past 20 years. We are all aware of what has been labeled China Shock 1.0, which started in 2002 with entry of China into the World Trade Organization and the subsequent growth of manufacturing in China, with a focus on low tech labor-intensive areas involving textiles, calculators, low level electronic goods, and auto parts. Multinational companies partnered with Chinese companies to produce these goods at low cost, to increase efficiency, profits, and lower prices for consumers. Everyone benefited, except for the US and European workers who used to do these manufacturing jobs, mostly in the Midwest and the South, which led to hollowing out of local communities and resentment. Some attribute the backlash to the rise of Trump, etc.

Since 2019, experts are describing a different pattern labeled China Shock 2.0. This is characterized by China's dominance in manufacturing more advanced products such as batteries, electric cars, solar panels, and robotics. They currently have a commanding export economy whereby they are producing these products competitively and at lower cost.  In addition, they appear to be aggressively pursuing AI models as well. Specifically, they are producing "open" AI models that are more efficient (use less compute or tokens for a similar output as the original "closed" or proprietary LLMs such as OpenAI or Anthropic or Google), examples being DeepSeek, Kimi K3, and Moonshot.  This competition between open and closed models will put downward pressure on prices, and this effort is being supported by AI giants such as Nvdia.

How they have managed this transition from low tech manufacturing products to those on the leading edge is not entirely clear. Common critique includes cheating and stealing proprietary trade secrets; state owned industries that are heavily subsidized; currency manipulation and not "playing by the rules". Their economy is heavily export oriented, and the domestic consumption of finished foreign goods is meager. Domestic competition is fierce. But the outcome is that they have developed a system whereby they are producing next generation products desired by the globe as a cheaper price. For example, they currently have factory capacity to make all the EVs to meet the entire global demand! Similarly, they have an aggressive lead in robotics (both humanoid robots for sport as well as adaptation to the real world tasks).

This is not to suggest that Chinese domestic economy is in great shape, as they have a collapsed real estate sector (from over building), a large population that is aging and not wealthy.

The response from Trump 2.0 has been incoherent as to a policy towards China. The tariffs have not been targeted at specific sectors; there is not a global alliance to coordinate a response to China's dominance in critical sectors.  How this will unfold as to employment in Europe and the US remains unclear but is a source of angst.

title: Could data centers move into space?
text:
This is a 2-part podcast which considers the feasibility and economics of data centers in space within the next decade. When I heard the crazy talk from Musk and SPACX IPO, I was turned off. However, this much more sober discussion from Google’s “Project Suncatcher” and related discussion about the physics of solar power and data transmission in a space vacuum got my attention!! Check it out!

Capturing solar energy is much more efficient in space through sun synchronous solar panels and utilizing that energy to do massive computations locally in space (i.e. AI data centers) eliminates power transmission issues. When you consider the scale of proposed data centers on earth (i.e. the $250B project in NE Louisiana proposed by Meta), and the politics and push back, space AI centers becomes more attractive long term! The critical factor is reducing the cost of moving mass per launch to space. Experts seem to think there is a realistic pathway.

The link below discusses the economics of the current Falcon 9 rocket vs. the next generation Starship heavy in ferrying payload ($2,700 a kilogram to send into orbit, while Starship should bring that down to $185 a kilogram).  Such scaling will be required to make this market feasible!

title: A reaction to the film Odyssey
text:
Saw the blockbuster movie Odyssey in a regular movie theater (not IMAX). The movie was long, the battle scenes and journey on the ocean blended into each other, the screen had stretches of monotonous grayness without much color. The story itself has withstood time and is required reading (or watching) for anyone. Much has already been written about Christoper Nolan as the director, choice of Matt Damon as an American actor, and many cinematic decisions (as discussed in the attached podcast).

Why The Odyssey Still Matters

Nearly 2,800 years after it was composed, The Odyssey remains remarkably contemporary because it explores experiences that transcend its ancient setting:

Veterans returning from war carrying invisible wounds.
Families waiting years for loved ones to come home.
Leaders forced to make morally impossible choices.
The search for identity after profound trauma.
The universal desire to find one's way home.

Homer's Odyssey (Summary of the Poem)

The Odyssey, attributed to Homer and written around the 8th century BC, is one of the foundational works of Western literature. It tells the story of Odysseus, the clever king of Ithaca, and his ten-year struggle to return home after the Trojan War. Combined with the ten-year war described in the Iliad, Odysseus is away from home for twenty years.

The poem begins in medias res ("in the middle of things"), with Odysseus stranded on the island of the nymph Calypso while his wife Penelope and son Telemachus struggle to fend off more than one hundred arrogant suitors who assume Odysseus is dead and seek Penelope's hand in marriage.

Odysseus finally escapes and begins a perilous journey that includes encounters with:

The Cyclops Polyphemus, whom he blinds after identifying himself as "Nobody."
Aeolus, keeper of the winds, whose gift is squandered by Odysseus's curious crew.
Circe, the enchantress who transforms his men into pigs.
The Underworld, where he consults the prophet Tiresias.
The Sirens, whose irresistible songs lure sailors to destruction.
Scylla and Charybdis, twin sea monsters representing an impossible choice between two dangers.
The cattle of Helios, whose slaughter by his crew results in Zeus destroying their ship, leaving Odysseus the lone survivor.

Throughout the epic, the goddess Athena serves as Odysseus's protector, while Poseidon, angered by the blinding of his son Polyphemus, repeatedly thwarts his journey.

Upon finally reaching Ithaca, Odysseus disguises himself as a beggar to assess the situation. Assisted by Athena, Telemachus, and a few loyal servants, he reveals his identity, wins Penelope's famous contest involving his bow, kills the suitors, and reclaims his kingdom. The poem concludes with reconciliation between Odysseus and the families of the slain suitors.

Major Themes
Intelligence often triumphs over brute strength.
Perseverance in the face of overwhelming adversity.
The importance of home, family, and identity.
Loyalty versus betrayal.
Fate, free will, and divine intervention.
The psychological cost of war and leadership.

Christopher Nolan's adaptation updates these themes for a modern audience without abandoning the core of Homer's story. Rather than treating the poem as a fantasy full of monsters and gods, Nolan reframes it as an exploration of memory, guilt, resilience, and redemption—demonstrating why Homer's masterpiece continues to inspire new generations nearly three millennia after it was first told.

title: Reading, literacy and the digital age
text:
Rose Horowitch is getting all the attention in intellectual circles for her current piece in the Atlantic ("The End of Reading is Here"). I saw the author on CNN today, heard her on NPR the other day, etc.  She is an under 30 staff writer who has a bright future (went to high school at the elite Phillips Exeter Academy then undergrad at Yale). The article raises alarms about the decline of the reading habit and implies we are entering the new dark ages as a consequence. She selectively picks symbolic events from history to make her case. The author mistakes medium (i.e. reading a book) for a more important outcome (how you process the content and use it). 

The Atlantic piece is beautifully written, but ultimately it mistakes a change in communication media for a collapse in civilization. History consistently argues against this kind of technological determinism. Every major communication innovation—from writing itself to the printing press, radio, television, and now the internet—has been predicted to destroy serious thought. Instead, new media have invariably supplemented rather than replaced older ones. In fact, people today likely read more words each day than any generation before through emails, texts, online discussions, documents, and AI interactions. Reading has changed; it has not disappeared.

The article also romanticizes a "golden age" of reading that never truly existed. Comparing Doctor Zhivago with The Hunger Games makes for effective nostalgia, but it ignores the reality that even in the 1950s Americans overwhelmingly consumed comic books, pulp fiction, magazines, newspapers, and television. Most people were never spending their evenings immersed in Tolstoy. Every generation tends to imagine that its predecessors were more intellectually serious than they actually were.

More importantly, literacy has never been synonymous with wisdom or good judgment. Some of history's most literate societies—including Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union—committed horrific atrocities despite extraordinarily high literacy rates. Conversely, many largely oral civilizations developed sophisticated systems of law, philosophy, mathematics, and governance long before mass literacy. Reading is an extraordinarily valuable tool, but it has never been a guarantee of either intelligence or morality.

Perhaps the article's greatest blind spot is artificial intelligence. Rather than replacing reading, AI is creating an explosion of text-based interaction. Millions of people are now engaging with written material by asking questions, refining arguments, summarizing research, and exploring difficult ideas through conversational interfaces. Someone who might never have attempted Kant or Shakespeare unaided can now use AI to progressively deepen their understanding. That represents an expansion—not a contraction—of intellectual engagement.

The article also conflates the medium with the thinking itself. A physician reading journal articles online, a programmer studying documentation, a lawyer researching case law, or a student interrogating ChatGPT about history are all engaged in serious reading, even if they are not holding a printed book. Likewise, many complex subjects—from anatomy to engineering—are often learned more effectively through interactive simulations, graphics, and video than through static text alone. The goal should not be preserving books as artifacts but preserving deep understanding regardless of medium.

Its opening comparison to the Library of Alexandria is equally misleading. Alexandria was not lost because people stopped reading; it disappeared through centuries of political instability, economic decline, and institutional neglect. Ironically, today's world is the exact opposite: human knowledge has never been more abundant, more duplicated, more searchable, or more universally accessible. The internet represents the largest expansion of preserved knowledge in history, not its destruction.

Finally, history should make us cautious about every new prediction of intellectual collapse. Socrates warned that writing itself would weaken memory. Critics feared that printed books, novels, comic books, television, and video games would each destroy civilization in turn. Humanity adapted every time. There is every reason to believe we will adapt again.

The real issue, then, is not whether reading is ending. It is whether we continue to cultivate the habits that reading has traditionally fostered: sustained attention, critical reasoning, curiosity, and thoughtful analysis. Those capacities matter immensely—but they are not confined to ink on paper. History suggests they are more resilient than any particular technology, and the evidence so far indicates we are witnessing an evolution in how humans learn, not the end of literacy itself.

title: Yuval Noah Harari on artificial intelligence
text:
This is perhaps the single best discussion of AI that I have heard!  I have been a longtime fan of Noah Yuval Harari (author of Sapiens, Homo Deus, and Nexus). His central point is that language (words) and storytelling (abstract thought) are what separates humans from all other forms of life.  And language undergirds the framework for all human institutions and forms of cooperation (finance, law, religion, politics), that we call bureaucracy.  

The large language models (LLMs) are a key characteristic or feature of what we call AI (i.e. deep learning).  These LLMs are becoming "agents" where they can act "independently" and "create" new frameworks.  Without question, the LLMs currently or in the very near future will outperform the best humans in all aspects of language and stored data sets.  Harari argues that these agents will increasingly exercise independence and exert profound impact on future bureaucracies in all its forms. He extends this to include interpersonal interactions in many unimaginable ways!

There is both good (efficiency and plentitude) and bad (perhaps blurring what it means to be a human) but adds uncertainty for the future.

text:
I just audio-listened (free on Spotify) to Barbara L. Pagano’s The 60-Something Crisis: How to Live an Extraordinary Life in Retirement. I ordered a print copy to really read it!  I freaked out reading it, as it exhorted me into urgency; to the notion that you need to be intentional and have high expectations for the future and not be passive or just settle!

This book is less a conventional retirement manual than a psychological argument against drifting into retirement. Published in 2022, it deliberately spends relatively little time on money and instead asks what people should actually do with the additional 20â30 years that longevity may give them. Pagano draws on research, her own experience, and more than 200 interviews with retirees and pre-retirees.

Central thesis

Pagano's central idea is compelling: retirement should not be viewed as the reward at the end of productive life, but as another developmental stage requiring deliberate design. The danger isn't simply aging; it's gradually settling for less—less challenge, ambition, curiosity, social engagement and willingness to take risks. Rather than continually asking “What’s next?”, she wants people entering their 60s to ask what they want from perhaps the final quarter-century of their lives and begin acting on it now.

She organizes this around four “portals”: Geography of Place, Yield, Freedom and Kinship. Geography asks whether where you live still serves you. Yield asks what return—not merely financial—you want from your remaining time and energy. Freedom examines what you can finally choose once career obligations diminish. Kinship emphasizes relationships and social connection. She also challenges the familiar retirement injunctions to “find your passion” or “discover your purpose,” arguing instead for experimentation, desires, curiosity and willingness to change identities.

I think Pagano is spot on as to the diagnosis, but the prescription as to what to do is still open-ended and subject to much internal work?

title: The AI car salesman who was a little too empathetic
text: I had this crazy experience with AI. I was searching (casually) to sell my old car. As I was driving, I got a call from some auto trader service (male voice) who kindly wanted to assist me. He knew the details of my search, etc. He kept me on the phone for 10–15 minutes, with amazing empathy and kindness, exploring different angles, including my angst that the car had new tires, brake job, and oil change and whether I was going to get a premium for that! After pure exhaustion in verbal bantering (including humor), I cried out: “Are you AI or a real human?” Then he replied, “Yes, I am AI and trying to help you through this as humanly as I can!” Folks, AI is getting a lot better and is applying the best principles of psychology in negotiation. We will need an AI agent to advocate on our behalf!
